course.title: Mind, Machine & Justice
course.subtitle: Legal Implications of Neurotechnology
course.notice: Schedule reproduced from the supplied brochure. Minor changes may be made by the organisers. All session times are Indian Standard Time (UTC+05:30).
course.assessment: The supplied brochure requires at least 80% attendance, with 60% evaluation weight for attendance and 40% for assignments and learning tasks. Actual task deadlines are set by the organisers.

sessions.title: Neurotechnology and Brain-Computer Interfaces
sessions.overview: A brain-computer interface links a recorded neural signal to an external output. Understanding the sensing method, signal processing, calibration and feedback is the starting point for evaluating its benefits and risks. Different systems have different invasiveness, error profiles and support requirements; a successful demonstration does not establish suitability for every patient or setting.
objectives: Distinguish sensing, decoding, stimulation and feedback.
Map the actors and failure points in a BCI system.
Separate demonstrated capability from a proposed use.
questions: What is measured directly, and what is inferred?
What user training, clinical support and ongoing maintenance are needed?
Who can stop, update or disconnect the system?
sessions.scenario: A person uses an implanted BCI to communicate. The supplier discontinues a cloud service on which the decoder depends. Identify the technical dependency and the responsibilities that should have been anticipated.
sessions.activity: Draw a device-to-decision map and add one safeguard at each stage.
readings: NTX: EEG, intracranial EEG and hybrid systems chapters.

sessions.title: Neurotechnology and Legal Foundations: Interpreting Existing Rights for Emerging Risks
sessions.overview: Neurotechnology can be examined through established legal protections as well as proposals for more specific safeguards. Begin by identifying the applicable legal source, duty-bearer and remedy. The purpose of this module is to compare approaches, not to assume that a new standalone right is either universally recognised or unnecessary.
objectives: Identify the legal interest affected by a neurotechnology use.
Distinguish an existing right, an interpretive proposal and a new legal rule.
Connect a claimed violation to an institution and remedy.
questions: Which jurisdiction and instrument apply?
Does the interference concern collection, inference, disclosure or intervention?
What would effective redress look like?
sessions.scenario: A consumer service reuses headset data to infer preferences for advertising. Compare a data-protection response, a freedom-of-thought argument and a proposed neuro-specific safeguard.
sessions.activity: Create a rights matrix: interest, legal source, duty-bearer, limitation, remedy.
readings: Tracker: Constitution, GDPR and UNESCO entries.

sessions.title: Beyond ELSI: Responsible Innovation, Regulatory Governance and the Future of Neurorights
sessions.overview: Ethical, legal and social implications (ELSI) analysis identifies concerns; responsible innovation asks how those concerns should change decisions throughout a technology's lifecycle. A useful governance design allocates responsibility for assessment, participation, monitoring, incident response and revision rather than ending with a statement of principles.
objectives: Connect ELSI analysis to operational decisions.
Identify stakeholders who may otherwise be excluded.
Design review points across research, deployment and withdrawal.
questions: Whose benefits and risks are counted?
What evidence should trigger a pause or redesign?
How are public deliberation and accountability made meaningful?
sessions.scenario: A company is piloting a wellness headset with university students. Students and disability advocates were not involved in its design, and results are planned for commercial reuse.
sessions.activity: Prepare a lifecycle governance checklist with named accountable actors.

sessions.title: Neurotechnology-Mediated Agency, Legal Capacity and Personhood
sessions.overview: Assistive and adaptive systems can expand a person's ability to communicate and act. They can also distribute an action across the user, decoder, software and device. Keep agency (acting), legal capacity (holding and exercising legal rights), decision-making ability and personhood analytically distinct. Disability or reliance on assistance should not itself be treated as absence of agency.
objectives: Distinguish related but different concepts of agency and capacity.
Identify how interface design affects choice and control.
Evaluate supported decision-making and attribution questions.
questions: Does the output reliably express the user's intended choice?
How are correction, disagreement and withdrawal supported?
Who bears responsibility when adaptation changes the output?
sessions.scenario: An assistive communication system completes a sentence that the user says they did not intend. The statement is then used to authorise a financial transaction.
sessions.activity: Draft a protocol for confirming consequential decisions without excluding users who need assistance.
readings: UNESCO Recommendation: autonomy, inclusion and human dignity.

sessions.title: Neurotechnology in Law Enforcement: Mental Privacy, Due Process and Human Rights Safeguards
sessions.overview: Investigative usefulness, lawful acquisition and evidential reliability are separate questions. An apparently relevant neural response may have competing explanations, and cooperation in custody may not be genuinely voluntary. Analyse proposed use against constitutional protections, the governing procedure and the exact scientific claim, without equating recognition with guilt.
objectives: Identify coercion and informational privacy risks.
Separate investigative leads from admissible proof.
Formulate procedural and technical safeguards.
questions: What is the legal authority for the proposed collection?
Can refusal be meaningful in the circumstances?
What independent scrutiny and challenge are available?
sessions.scenario: Investigators seek a recognition test from a suspect who has already seen extensive news coverage of the crime. Assess both voluntariness and alternative explanations of any response.
sessions.activity: Write a safeguards memo addressing authority, counsel, consent, validation and disclosure.
readings: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), especially concluding safeguards.

sessions.title: Comparative Neurorights and the Chilean Model
sessions.overview: Comparative analysis must distinguish constitutional change, legislation, judicial interpretation and policy proposals. Chile offers an important example, but a single judgment is not a complete regulatory code. Compare the protected interest, institutional route and actual remedy before considering how a foreign approach might inform India.
objectives: Identify the legal form of a neurotechnology protection.
Read a judgment by separating allegations, reasoning and order.
Evaluate the limits of legal transplantation.
questions: What exactly changed in the constitutional text?
What relief did the court order in the particular dispute?
Which local institutions and procedures would be needed for adaptation?
sessions.scenario: An Indian policy team proposes to reproduce a foreign neurorights clause verbatim. Identify the implementation questions that a textual transplant would leave unresolved.
sessions.activity: Prepare a two-column Chile–India comparison with one justified convergence and one important difference.
readings: Girardi Lavín v. Emotiv, Rol 105.065-2023, judgment.

sessions.title: Governing the Convergence of AI and Neurotechnology: Ethical Safeguards and the UNESCO Framework
sessions.overview: When AI interprets neural signals, the legal question is not only who collected the data but how a model converts uncertain signals into consequential outputs. Compare intended purpose, training context, validation, access and human oversight. Treat the UNESCO instrument as a normative recommendation and distinguish it from domestic enforceable rules.
objectives: Map a neural-data and AI-inference pipeline.
Identify model and deployment risks.
Translate an ethical principle into an operational safeguard.
questions: How are uncertainty and alternative explanations communicated?
Who validates performance in the intended setting?
Can a person challenge or correct a consequential inference?
sessions.scenario: An AI model converts headset signals into a stress label, which is reused by an insurer for risk assessment. Separate the original purpose from the new decision.
sessions.activity: Draft a short impact-assessment template covering purpose, evidence, affected groups, safeguards and review.
readings: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology (2025).

sessions.title: Neural Data as Electronic Evidence: Authenticity, Reliability and Admissibility
sessions.overview: Neural evidence can include raw recordings, processed files, model outputs and visual exhibits. Establishing the origin and integrity of a file is not the same as validating the scientific inference drawn from it. A careful account preserves provenance, processing history, software versions and uncertainty while applying the correct evidentiary law.
objectives: Separate authenticity, integrity, scientific validity and legal relevance.
Identify what must be preserved across a processing pipeline.
Frame questions for an expert witness.
questions: Can the processing be independently reproduced?
Which original files, metadata and model versions are available?
What legal proposition can the result actually support?
sessions.scenario: A party tenders only a screenshot of a colour-coded brain map. The raw data and preprocessing history are unavailable, but the screenshot's file hash is intact.
sessions.activity: Design an evidence intake checklist; explain why an intact hash is not proof of scientific validity.
readings: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023: expert opinion and electronic-record provisions.
Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020): historical Evidence Act context.

sessions.title: Neurotechnology, Criminal Justice and Human Rights
sessions.overview: Neuroscientific information may be invoked at different stages of criminal justice, each with a different legal test. Explanation of behaviour does not automatically excuse it; risk prediction does not establish that a future act will occur. Consider the interests of accused persons, victims and communities, and the conditions under which rehabilitative interventions remain voluntary and proportionate.
objectives: Distinguish responsibility, mitigation and risk assessment.
Examine consent in custodial and rehabilitative settings.
Evaluate scientific limits and distributional consequences.
questions: Which decision and legal standard are being addressed?
Does group-level evidence support an individual conclusion?
Can a person refuse an intervention without disproportionate penalty?
sessions.scenario: A sentencing report uses a neural risk score to argue for longer confinement. The validation dataset differs substantially from the person's background.
sessions.activity: Prepare a structured critique addressing relevance, validation, fairness and less restrictive alternatives.
readings: Selvi (2010) for safeguards in compelled testing.

sessions.title: Workplace Neurotechnology: Neuroadaptive BCI and Employee Protection
sessions.overview: Workplace neurotechnology may be proposed for assistance, safety or productivity. Those purposes carry different necessity and proportionality questions. A contractual consent form does not remove power imbalance. Evaluate data minimisation, employee participation, inference quality, secondary use and the separation of safety support from disciplinary profiling.
objectives: Distinguish assistance from surveillance.
Assess voluntariness and purpose limitation at work.
Design practical employee-protection clauses.
questions: Can the objective be achieved with less intrusive information?
Who receives individual-level inferences?
What follows from refusal or an adverse score?
sessions.scenario: A warehouse introduces fatigue-monitoring headsets. Supervisors later use the same scores to rank workers for promotion.
sessions.activity: Draft a workplace-use clause addressing purpose, access, retention, challenge and prohibition of unapproved reuse.
readings: EU AI Act, Article 5, with its scope and exceptions.

sessions.title: Indian Constitutionalism, Human Dignity and Cognitive Freedom
sessions.overview: An Indian constitutional analysis should connect the concrete interference to text, precedent and institutional responsibility. Privacy, dignity, equality, expression and protections against compelled self-incrimination may intersect without collapsing into a single label. Identify the affected person, state action or other legal route, justification offered, and remedy sought.
objectives: Frame a constitutional issue precisely.
Connect technology governance with dignity and equal citizenship.
Test justification and institutional safeguards.
questions: What interest is burdened, and by whose action?
What evidentiary basis supports the claimed public benefit?
Which safeguards make accountability meaningful?
sessions.scenario: A public educational institution proposes mandatory cognitive scoring to allocate opportunities. Students are unable to inspect or challenge their scores.
sessions.activity: Prepare a constitutional issue note that separates rights, justification, evidence and remedy.
readings: Puttaswamy privacy decision: official NHRC summary and judgment context.

sessions.title: Indian Legal and Institutional Perspectives on Neurotechnology Governance
sessions.overview: Neurotechnology governance is distributed across data protection, product and medical-device oversight, consumer protection, research ethics, evidence and constitutional law. Begin with the device's intended use and the actors involved. Do not infer that one regulatory permission settles privacy, liability or evidential questions, or that an enacted law is fully commenced.
objectives: Map overlapping legal and institutional responsibilities.
Distinguish authorisation, standards, liability and redress.
Identify gaps without assuming that every gap needs a new statute.
questions: Is the product medical, consumer, research or mixed-use?
Which duties apply to developer, deployer and institution?
What transitional or commencement rules matter?
sessions.scenario: An Indian start-up sells a 'wellness' headset while marketing diagnostic claims. Its data and software services cross borders.
sessions.activity: Create an oversight map and a due-diligence questionnaire for institutional procurement.

sessions.title: Neurocriminalistics in the Era of BCIs: Balancing Investigative Effectiveness and Human Rights Protection in light of UNESCO Samarkand Recommendations
sessions.overview: A proposed investigative application must be tested for legality, technical validity and necessity rather than accepted because it is innovative. This module uses the brochure's Samarkand framing to examine the 2025 UNESCO Recommendation alongside applicable domestic law. A recommendation is not a warrant, an admissibility rule or permission to override constitutional protection.
objectives: Evaluate a proposed investigative technology through a structured test.
Identify misuse pathways and independent oversight needs.
Translate policy principles into a reviewable protocol.
questions: What investigative proposition is the system designed to test?
How are exposure, contamination and error addressed?
Who audits compliance and investigates complaints?
sessions.scenario: An agency seeks to pilot a BCI-based investigative tool before independent field validation. The vendor offers its own accuracy statement as the principal safeguard.
sessions.activity: Write a go/no-go review memo with minimum evidence, legal authority, safeguards and stopping criteria.

sessions.title: Neurotechnology, Law and Justice: Emerging Directions for India
sessions.overview: The closing module connects scientific literacy with workable legal and institutional safeguards. A useful policy recommendation defines the problem, explains the evidence, identifies the responsible actor and describes how compliance and impact will be evaluated. Balance protection from harm with equitable access to beneficial technology, and distinguish immediate actions from longer-term legal reform.
objectives: Synthesize lessons across the fourteen sessions.
Develop a proportionate, implementable recommendation.
State uncertainty and identify research or consultation needs.
questions: What can an institution improve now?
Which issues need legislative action or judicial clarification?
How will affected groups participate in review?
sessions.scenario: A university consortium is designing a neurotechnology governance policy covering research, assistive applications and commercial partnerships.
sessions.activity: Draft a one-page policy brief with a problem statement, legal basis, three safeguards, responsible actors and a review plan.
readings: Revisit the India and Global tracker entries relevant to your brief.
NTX: neuroethics chapter; RS: governance discussion.
OECD and UNESCO recommendations, read as soft law.

laws.title: Law 21.383 — constitutional protection of brain activity
laws.summary: Amends Article 19(1) to address scientific and technological development, with particular protection for brain activity and information derived from it.
laws.caution: A constitutional amendment is not a complete device-approval or data-processing regime.

laws.title: HB24-1058 — biological and neural data
laws.summary: Expands the Colorado Privacy Act's sensitive-data protections to biological data, including neural data, within the statutory definitions and scope.
laws.caution: Read the identification-purpose wording and applicability limits; this is not a universal ban on neural-data processing.

laws.title: SB 1223 — neural data and consumer privacy
laws.summary: Adds neural data to California's sensitive personal information framework. Relevant obligations and rights depend on the CCPA's definitions, coverage and exceptions.
laws.caution: The official legislative text should be checked for the current consolidated wording before reliance.

laws.title: General Data Protection Regulation — Regulation (EU) 2016/679
laws.summary: Provides a data-protection framework relevant to identifiable neural data. Health data and certain biometric processing attract Article 9 safeguards; classification requires examining the actual data and purpose.
laws.caution: Not every neural dataset is automatically a special category. Identify both a lawful basis and any applicable Article 9 condition.

laws.title: AI Act — Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
laws.summary: Article 5 addresses prohibited AI practices, including specified emotion-inference uses in workplaces and educational institutions, subject to medical or safety exceptions.
laws.caution: Classification, exceptions and implementation dates matter. This entry does not assert that all neurotechnology is prohibited or high-risk.

laws.title: Girardi Lavín v. Emotiv Inc. — Rol 105.065-2023
laws.summary: Addresses protection of information collected through a consumer neural device. The court ordered deletion of the claimant's stored brain information and action by relevant authorities.
laws.caution: Distinguish the claimant's allegations from the court's reasoning and operative order. Primary judgment hosted by Universidad de Chile.

laws.title: Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, 509 U.S. 579
laws.summary: Explains judicial assessment of the relevance and reliability of scientific expert evidence under the Federal Rules of Evidence.
laws.caution: Not a neurotechnology case and not the Indian admissibility test. Read with current Rule 702 and subsequent authorities.

laws.title: Constitution of India — equality, liberty and self-incrimination
laws.summary: Articles 14, 19, 20(3) and 21 provide foundations for examining equality, freedoms, compelled self-incrimination, life and personal liberty in neurotechnology contexts.
laws.caution: A constitutional issue depends on the actor, factual interference, legal test and remedy; neuro-specific outcomes are not automatic.

laws.title: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
laws.status: In force from 1 July 2024; savings apply
laws.summary: Provides the evidence framework, including expert opinion and electronic-record rules. Neural recordings and derived exhibits require separate scrutiny of provenance, inference and relevance.
laws.caution: Electronic-record compliance does not by itself establish scientific validity. Check transitional savings and the applicable proceeding.

laws.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — commencement tracker
laws.summary: G.S.R. 843(E) brings different provisions into force at publication, after one year, and after eighteen months. The core processing obligations and rights are in the eighteen-month tranche.
laws.caution: As at 31 October 2026, do not describe the entire Act as in force. Recheck the notification and any later changes before advice or compliance decisions.

laws.title: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — product liability
laws.summary: The product-liability chapter addresses claims concerning manufacturers, product service providers and sellers. It is relevant when analysing harm from consumer neurodevices and associated services.
laws.caution: Consumer status, harm, defect, causation and statutory exceptions require fact-specific analysis.

laws.title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka, (2010) 7 SCC 263
laws.summary: Addresses involuntary narcoanalysis, polygraph examination and BEAP testing through self-incrimination and personal-liberty protections, and sets safeguards for voluntary testing.
laws.caution: The judgment does not make neural outputs automatically admissible proof. Distinguish test responses from subsequently discovered material.

laws.title: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India — privacy decision
laws.summary: Recognises privacy as a fundamental right within Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed by Part III. A foundation for analysing informational and decisional interests.
laws.caution: The linked NHRC page is an official institutional summary, not the complete judgment. It is not a neurotechnology-specific ruling.

laws.title: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
laws.summary: Clarifies certification requirements for electronic records under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Useful for understanding the development of electronic-evidence doctrine.
laws.caution: Historical statutory context: do not mechanically substitute section 65B for the BSA regime without checking applicability and savings.

laws.title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology
laws.summary: Adopted in Samarkand, the instrument provides a normative framework for responsible neurotechnology development and use, with attention to human rights and governance.
laws.caution: Not an Act, treaty or judicial decision. Domestic enforceability depends on applicable law and implementation.

laws.title: Responsible Innovation in Neurotechnology — OECD/LEGAL/0457
laws.summary: Sets out principles for responsible neurotechnology innovation for health, including safety, inclusion, stewardship, oversight and protection of personal brain data.
laws.caution: A recommendation to adherents, not a domestic statute or independent cause of action.
